paper_summary: Cinar (Eur. J. Eng. App. Sci. 2022) develops a syntactic foam from MGS R285/H285 epoxy filled with 56 wt% expanded (porous) recycled-glass granules of 1-2 mm, and uses it as a filler core inside 6060-T6 aluminum circular tubes (20 mm OD, 1 mm wall, 25 mm high). Quasi-static axial compression tests compare empty base tubes (BT), bare syntactic foam (SF) and foam-filled tubes (FFT). Foam filling changed the tube collapse mode from diamond to ring/concertina, and the foam-filled tube absorbed more energy than the sum of the separate tube and foam, indicating a tube-foam interaction effect; the addition of the foam raised specific absorbed energy by 42% and absorbed energy by 188%.

structure.microstructure_notes: Filler is expanded glass in the form of small porous spheres, particle size 1-2 mm, crush strength 1.5-2.5 MPa. Micrographs show microvoids inside the expanded glass particles and macro voids between them; after compression the spheres are crushed and elongated. Specimens turned to 18 mm outer diameter and 25 mm height; three samples per configuration.

test.specimen_notes: Quasi-static axial compression, cylindrical foam specimen 18 mm diameter x 25 mm high, total compression displacement 20 mm (values considered up to the compaction region). Load-displacement curve shows linear, plateau and densification regions; failure initiates by shear deformation followed by material separation.

extraction_notes:
MAJOR CAVEAT: this 5-page short paper reports essentially all of its measured mechanical results in figures only. Load-displacement curves (Fig. 2), the interaction-effect area (Fig. 4) and the specific absorbed energy / absorbed energy bar charts (Fig. 6) carry no numeric values in the text, and there is no results table. Consequently no modulus, strength, plateau stress, densification strain or energy absorption value could be extracted for the syntactic foam, the base tube or the foam-filled tube - only the relative improvements '42% higher specific absorbed energy' and '188% higher absorbed energy' for the foam-filled tube versus the empty tube are stated, which cannot be converted to absolute schema units. Those fields are left null per the no-invented-numbers rule.

PARTICLE TYPE: the filler is expanded (foamed) recycled glass granules, i.e. porous rather than single-cavity hollow microballoons, and is coarse (1-2 mm) compared with typical microballoons, so particle_type is set to 'other' rather than glass_microballoon. The paper nevertheless calls the material a syntactic foam throughout, so is_syntactic_foam_paper=true.

DENSITY AMBIGUITY: Table 1 lists the expanded glass 'Density (kg/m3) 230' without stating whether this is the poured bulk density of the granules or the true particle density; it is recorded as particle_true_density_g_cc = 0.23 (230 kg/m3 / 1000) with this caveat.

COMPOSITION: only a mass (weight) fraction of 56% expanded glass is reported; no volume fraction is given and no conversion was attempted, so particle_volume_fraction is null. Particle size is given only as a 1-2 mm range with no mean, so particle_mean_diameter_um is null and the range is recorded in microstructure_notes.

NOT EXTRACTED AS RECORDS: the 6060-T6 aluminum tube properties in Table 2 (yield 195 MPa, tensile 230 MPa, E 69 GPa, elongation 12%) describe the metal tube, not a hollow-particle composite, and the base tube (BT) and foam-filled tube (FFT) configurations are structural assemblies rather than foam compositions; none of these produced usable material-property numbers anyway. The neat cured resin record is supplier datasheet data (Ref. [26]) included as a filler-free matrix baseline and marked secondary; particle_type there is 'other' at zero fraction only because the schema requires a particle type.

UNIT CONVERSIONS: elastic modulus 3.2 GPa -> 3200 MPa; expanded glass density 230 kg/m3 -> 0.23 g/cm3.
